cultivar: Local Baojing Huangjin population; selections include Baojing Huangjin Cha No. 1 and No. 2
processing: Made as a green tea: fixed, rolled, shaped into straight strips and dried. The leaf itself is what sets it apart, being unusually high in amino acids.
harvest_season: Spring. The selected cultivars bud early, and as with other Chinese green teas the earliest tender pickings are the prized ones.
appearance_wet: Tender green buds and leaves, as is typical of an early-picked green tea.
taste_profile: Strong fresh aroma and a crisp, brothy cup with a sweet aftertaste; the high amino acid content gives it more savoury depth than most greens.

brewing.notes: General green tea advice: cooler water protects the sweetness. Too hot or too long brings up the bitterness that its high polyphenol content can give.

vintage_note: Sold as the current year's spring green tea, and as with green tea generally it is best within the year. Earlier and more tender lots command higher prices. Producers also make a black tea from the same leaf, which is sold separately.
description:
Baojing Huangjin Cha means Baojing gold tea, and despite the name it is a green tea, from Baojing County in the Xiangxi prefecture of western Hunan. The gold is a matter of price and pride: the local saying has it that a measure of this tea is worth the same measure of gold.

What makes it distinct is the plant. It comes from an old local tea population, whose leaf is high in amino acids, roughly twice ordinary green tea by local accounts, as well as polyphenols, water extract and chlorophyll.

The cup is the payoff: strong aroma, bright green liquor, a crisp taste and a sweet finish. Use water around 80 degrees and do not leave the leaf sitting, since a leaf this rich in polyphenols can turn sharp if pushed.

The label to check is the county. Baojing Huangjin Cha and the wider Xiangxi Huangjin Cha are both protected names. Ask for the place and the harvest date.
history:
Tea growing in Huangjin Village is the root of the story. The village keeps 2,057 old tea trees, the oldest reckoned at 419 years. The old garden and its tea culture are recognised as a China Important Agricultural Heritage System, and the traditional making methods are on Hunan's intangible heritage list.

The name holds a geographical indication certification trademark and is on the China-EU geographical indication list, and in 2025 Baojing was named among 54 national demonstration zones for geographical indication protection.
